(2) Model building¶

Different classifiers to try out during grid search¶

In this section we will 3 types of classifiers and decide which classifier will be more effective in detecting deafaults

Find the optimal hyperparameters for each classifier¶

Class imbalance is handled with a combination of 2 resampling techniques

  • SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique):
    SMOTE creates new synthetic points in order to have an equal balance of the classes. To achieve this, it takes an instance from the minority class and considers its k nearest neighbours in feature space, interpolates linearly along the segment between this instance and one of its k neighbors, then adds this new vector to the current instance to generate the new, synthetic data point.
  • ENN (Embedded Nearset Neighbours):
    This rule involves using k=3 nearest neighbors to locate those examples in a dataset that are misclassified and that are then removed before a k=1 classification rule is applied. The modified 3NN rule uses the 3-nearest neighbor rule to edit the pre-classified samples and then uses a single-nearest neighbor rule to make decisions. For each instance a in the dataset, its three nearest neighbors are computed. If a is a majority class instance and is misclassified by its three nearest neighbors, then a is removed from the dataset. Alternatively, if a is a minority class instance and is misclassified by its three nearest neighbors, then the majority class instances among a’s neighbors are removed.

Hyperparameter tuning

  • Grid search with cross-validation carried out to find optimal model settings (maximise ROC AUC)
  • The best models are refitted on the whole training sample and saved down as pickle object for easy access

Cross Validation with re-sampling:¶

Overfitting during Cross Validation: When re-sampling (undersampling or over-sampling) is performed on the training data, it must not be done before implementing cross-validation, as it would directly affect the validation set, leading to a "data leakage" problem and probably overfitting.

The Wrong Way¶


Let's assume we are splitting the data into 5 folds, 4/5 of the dataset will be the training set while 1/5 will be the validation set. The test set should remain separate from the training set and not used in the process of generating synthetic observations. For this reason, we have to perform the oversampling inside the cross-validation loop and not outside of it, just like below:

The Correct Way¶


Here oversampling occurs "during" cross validation and not "prior" to the cross validation process. Synthetic datapoints are created only for the training set without affecting the validation set.

In [25]:
# Feature selection libraries
from sklearn.feature_selection import f_classif, mutual_info_classif, chi2, SelectKBest, RFE, RFECV
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# Classification Libraries
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesClassifier, RandomForestClassifier

# Other sklearn Libraries
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, StandardScaler, RobustScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold

# Imbalance libraries
from imblearn.combine import SMOTEENN
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE, ADASYN

from pprint import pprint

reload(clf_lib)

SEP = '\n' + '-'*40 + '\n'
SEED = 42

# number of features to select before training a classifier
N_FEATURES = 20

# 5 fold stratified cross validation used for hyperparameter tuning
skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, random_state=SEED, shuffle=True)

# define resampling method
sampler = SMOTEENN(sampling_strategy='all',
                   smote=SMOTE(sampling_strategy='minority', k_neighbors=5, random_state=SEED),
                   random_state=SEED)

# sampler = ADASYN(sampling_strategy='all', n_neighbors=5, random_state=SEED)

Model evaluation terminology:¶

  • True Positives: Number of instances correctly classified as default
  • False Positives: Number of instances incorrectly classified as default
  • True Negative: Number of items correctly classified as non-default
  • False Negative: Number of items incorrectly classified as non-default
  • Total positives: P = TP + FN Number of instances labelled as default
  • Total negatives: N = FP + TN Number of instances labelled as non-default
  • Recall or Sensitivity or TPR (True Positive Rate): TP/(TP+FN) Percentage of instances correctly classified as default out of total defaults
  • Specificity or TNR (True Negative Rate): TN/(FP+TN) Percentage of instances correctly classified as non-default out of total non-defaults
  • Precision: TP/(TP+FP) Percentage of correctly classified instances out of total instances classified as default
  • FPR (False Positive Rate) or Type I Error: FP/(FP+TN) Percentage of instances wrongly classified as default out of total non-defaults
  • FNR (False Negative Rate) or Type II Error: FN/(TP+FN) Percentage of instances wrongly classified as non-default out of total defaults
  • Accuracy: (TP+TN)/(N+P) Percentage of total items classified correctly
  • F1 Score: Harmonic mean of precision and recall given by F1 = 2*Precision*Recall/(Precision+Recall)
  • Log-loss: A measure of accuracy that incorporates the idea of probabilistic confidence given by following expression for binary class: y*(y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p))
  • Balanced Accuracy Score: A measure of classification accuracy that takes into account class imbalance. It is defined as the average of recall obtained on each class. In the binary case, balanced accuracy is equal to the arithmetic mean of sensitivity and specificity, or the area under the ROC curve with binary predictions rather than scores (TPR + TNR)/2

(2.1) Logistic Regression¶

In [40]:
# Define feature selection method
feature_selector = SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=N_FEATURES)

clf_params = {
    'classifier'   : LogisticRegression(),
    'penalty'      : ['l1','l2','elasticnet'],
    'C'            : [0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1, 1.01, 1.05, 1.1, 1.15, 1.2],
    'solver'       : ['lbfgs'],
    'fit_intercept': [True, False]
}
best_model, best_params, score = clf_lib.tune_model_hyperparams(clf_params,
                                                                sampler,
                                                                feature_selector,
                                                                Xtrain,
                                                                ytrain,
                                                                cv=skf)

print(f'{SEP}<<< Champion Model Score = %{100*score:.2f} >>>{SEP}')

print(f'{SEP}<<< Selected Features >>>{SEP}')
support = best_model.named_steps['selector'].get_support(indices=True)
betas = best_model.named_steps['classifier'].coef_.flatten()
feature_coeffs = pd.Series(index=Xtrain.columns[support], data=betas)
if best_params['classifier__fit_intercept']==True:
    feature_coeffs['intercept'] = best_model.named_steps['classifier'].intercept_[0]
feature_coeffs = feature_coeffs.reindex(feature_coeffs.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)
print(feature_coeffs.rename('beta'))

print(f'{SEP}<<< Champion Model Specs >>>{SEP}')
print(pprint(best_params))

# Evaluate model on training sample with cross-validation
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14,5))
plt.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.6, wspace=0.6)

lr_results = clf_lib.evaluate_classifier_CV(best_model,
                                            X=Xtrain,
                                            y=ytrain,
                                            cv=skf,
                                            display=True,
                                            axs=axs,
                                            title='Logistic Regression\n')

print(f'{SEP}<<< Performance on Train set with CV >>>{SEP}')
print(lr_results)

# save down model config for later use
with open(f'optimal_hyperparams/LogisticRegression.p', 'wb') as fp:
    pickle.dump(best_model, fp, protocol=pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL)

                                                                Xtrain,
                                                                ytrain,
                                                                cv=skf)

print(f'{SEP}<<< Champion Model Score = %{100*score:.2f} >>>{SEP}')

print(f'{SEP}<<< Selected Features >>>{SEP}')
support = best_model.named_steps['selector'].get_support(indices=True)
print('\n'.join(Xtrain.columns[support]))

print(f'{SEP}<<< Champion Model Specs >>>{SEP}')
print(pprint(best_params))

# Evaluate model on training sample with cross-validation
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14,5))
plt.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.6, wspace=0.6)

rf_results = clf_lib.evaluate_classifier_CV(best_model,
                                            X=Xtrain,
                                            y=ytrain,
                                            cv=skf,
                                            display=True,
                                            axs=axs,
                                            title='Random Forest\n')

print(f'{SEP}<<< Performance on Train set with CV >>>{SEP}')
print(rf_results)

# save down model config for later use
with open(f'optimal_hyperparams/RandomForest.p', 'wb') as fp:
    pickle.dump(best_model, fp, protocol=pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL)

(3) Compare Model Performance on test sample¶

Here we can see that the decision tree model achieves the best recall (91.3%), i.e. is the best at correctly identifying default instances. However, it misclassifies 21.1% of instances in the test sample as default (FPR).

  • In terms of overall accuracy, random forest is our winning model with 84.8% accuracy on the test samle
  • In terms of area under the ROC curve and the balanced accuracy, decision tree model outperforms with a score of 90.2% and 85.1% respectively on the test sample

Drawing conclusions regarding the best model in this scenario depends on priorities and cost of misclassification. If it is more important to detect default (at the expense of a few more false positives) then decision tree is the best model. On the other hand, if the bank is more concerned about losing potentially good customers to whom the model gives a high probability of default, then random forest should be depolyed.
